_about: Sources opened for courses that are designed but not yet built. scripts/build_sources.py adds each entry to the listed keys of standards/sources.json with origin "planned course design", until the course goes live and its SOURCES.md takes over. Open every page before adding it. Fields: title, url, publisher, description (the facts it supports), license (null = not checked), reuse, checked (date opened), url_status, keys (defaults to the course keys).

sources.title: RFC 791: Internet Protocol
sources.description: IPv4: every packet carries a source and a destination address; addresses are four octets (32 bits); routers forward datagrams hop by hop. Weeks 2 and 3.

sources.title: RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
sources.description: IPv6 grows the address from 32 bits to 128 bits. Week 3 (address space, scalability).
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets
sources.description: The three private address blocks (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) used inside home and school networks. Week 3.
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
sources.description: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission, and opens a connection with a three-way handshake. Week 4.
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol
sources.description: UDP sends messages "with a minimum of protocol mechanism"; delivery and ordering are not guaranteed. Week 4 (TCP versus UDP tradeoff).
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 4271: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
sources.description: BGP is the inter-Autonomous System routing protocol that networks use to exchange reachability. Week 6 (how ISPs connect).
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names, Concepts and Facilities
sources.description: DNS is a hierarchical, distributed name space; resolvers ask name servers and cache answers. Week 1 and week 5.
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.description: Requests, methods (GET), status codes (200, 404) and the http and https URI schemes. Week 1 and week 9.
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.description: Caches store responses and reuse them to cut latency and load. Week 11 (scalability).
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
sources.description: TLS lets client and server talk "in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery"; the handshake authenticates the server and agrees on keys. Week 9 (HTTPS).
sources.license: IETF Trust and the document authors (RFC copyright notice); text may be quoted with credit, code components under the Revised BSD License

sources.title: Root Servers
sources.description: The DNS root zone is served by 13 named authorities (a to m.root-servers.net), each run on many servers, hundreds in all, in many countries. Week 5.

sources.title: Number Resources
sources.description: IANA allocates pools of unallocated IP addresses to the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and also manages Autonomous System Numbers. Weeks 3 and 6.

sources.title: What Does ICANN Do?
sources.description: Internet addresses must be unique; ICANN coordinates these unique identifiers worldwide. Week 5.

sources.title: CS101 Networking (Introduction)
sources.description: Bandwidth in bits per second (100 megabits, 1 gigabit); bits on a wire travel at about 2/3 the speed of light. Weeks 2 and 7.

sources.title: CS101 The Internet
sources.description: The Internet runs on the free, open, vendor-neutral TCP/IP standards; packets cross many routers (hop counts from Stanford). Weeks 2, 3 and 6.

sources.title: Submarine Cables
sources.description: "Over 95 percent of international data and voice transfers" go through seafloor fiber optic cables, not satellites; cable treaties date from 1884. Week 7.

sources.title: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits
sources.description: Low, medium and high Earth orbit; geosynchronous orbit is 42,164 km from Earth's center (about 36,000 km up); semi-synchronous about 20,200 km up. Week 8 (satellite latency). The URL now redirects to science.nasa.gov.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: CODATA Value: speed of light in vacuum
sources.description: c = 299 792 458 m/s (exact). The constant behind every latency figure (fiber, cable, satellite). Weeks 7 and 8.

sources.title: Broadband Speed Guide
sources.description: Minimum download speeds in Mbps per activity (browsing 1, HD video 5 to 8, 4K video 25); the FCC calls them rough guidelines. Week 6 (ISPs and the last mile).

sources.description: The 5.925 to 7.125 GHz band is open to unlicensed devices such as Wi-Fi (Report and Order, April 2020). Week 8 (Wi-Fi and cellular radio).

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B, Authentication and Authenticator Management
sources.description: Authentication assurance levels; AAL2 needs two distinct factors; phishing-resistant authenticators. Week 10.

sources.title: Phishing (Small Business Cybersecurity Corner)
sources.description: Phishing uses convincing messages to trick people into opening harmful links or giving up credentials; warning signs such as urgency. Week 10.

sources.title: FIPS 197, Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
sources.description: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 each encrypt 128-bit blocks; the number is the key length in bits. Week 9.

sources.title: Cybersecurity Framework
sources.description: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0) organizes security work into functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). Week 12 (security recommendations).

sources.title: Understanding Denial-of-Service Attacks
sources.description: DoS floods a system with illegitimate traffic; DDoS uses many devices (botnets); symptoms and responses. Weeks 10 and 11 (3A-NI-05).

sources.title: More than a Password (multifactor authentication)
sources.description: MFA uses two or more of something you know, have or are; phishing-resistant MFA is strongest. Weeks 10 and 12 (3A-NI-06, 3A-NI-07).

sources.title: Recognize and Report Phishing
sources.description: Signs of phishing (urgent language, requests for personal information, suspicious links) and what to do. Week 10.

sources.title: Internet History
sources.description: Timeline from ARPA and the ARPANET to the Internet. Week 1 (why the Internet is built from packets). Text and images © Computer History Museum.
sources.license: All rights reserved (© Computer History Museum)

sources.title: CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards, Revised 2017 (all levels, with descriptive statements)
sources.description: Level 2 text for 2-CS-01 to 2-CS-03 (devices, hardware and software that collect and exchange data, troubleshooting) and 2-AP-10 to 2-AP-17 (algorithms, control structures, decomposition, testing). Every week.

sources.title: What Is Robotics? (Grades 5-8)
sources.description: Robots are machines that do jobs; some work by themselves (autonomous), others need a person; rovers follow commands sent from Earth. Week 1.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Exploring Robotics, Unit D: Sensing and Decision Making (CISC 1003 lecture)
sources.publisher: Brooklyn College, City University of New York
sources.description: Sensor types (touch, light, infrared, ultrasonic); ultrasonic distance comes from time of flight; sensors give signals that a program turns into decisions. Weeks 2 and 3.

sources.title: Motion Sensors Explainer
sources.description: Accelerometer and gyroscope: what each measures. Week 2 and week 8 (how a drone knows it is tilting).

sources.title: Mars 2020 Perseverance rover components
sources.description: The rover's Inertial Measurement Unit gives 3-axis motion data and tilt; six Hazard Avoidance Cameras spot rocks, trenches and dunes. Weeks 2 and 6. (Opened as mars.nasa.gov/mars2020/spacecraft/rover/autonav/, which redirects here.)
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Understanding Space, Chapter 4.3.1: Space Vehicle Control Systems
sources.publisher: NASA Small Spacecraft Systems Virtual Institute (S3VI) knowledge base
sources.description: Open-loop versus closed-loop (feedback) control; in a thermostat the thermometer is the sensor, the thermostat the controller, the furnace the actuator. Week 4. Do not reuse its 20 C (75 F) example: 20 C is 68 F.

sources.title: Ingenuity Landing Press Kit: Mission Spacecraft
sources.description: Ingenuity: about 1.8 kg on Earth; four carbon-fiber blades in two 1.2 m counter-rotating rotors at about 2,400 rpm; a downward navigation camera; flights of up to 90 s and about 5 m up. Weeks 8 and 9.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
sources.description: First powered, controlled flight on another planet (April 19, 2021); 72 flights; last flight Jan. 18, 2024. Week 9.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Advanced Air Mobility: The Science Behind Quadcopters, Reader Student Guide
sources.description: Propellers push air down and the air pushes the drone up (Newton's third law); total lift is the sum of four propellers; tilting the lift moves the drone sideways; two propellers spin clockwise and two counterclockwise so their torques cancel, and speeding one pair turns (yaws) the drone; the worked 4 N quadcopter rules. Weeks 7 and 8.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: What is Lift?
sources.description: Lift opposes weight; it comes from a solid turning a moving flow of air (Newton's third law); no motion, no lift. Week 7.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: What is Thrust?
sources.description: Thrust is a mechanical force made by accelerating a mass of air or gas; it is a vector with size and direction. Week 7.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Propeller Thrust
sources.description: The engine turns the propeller, which does work on the air, so pressure changes abruptly across the propeller disk; blades are twisted from hub to tip. Week 7 (qualitative only at this level).
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Torque (Moment)
sources.description: Torque is the product of a force and its perpendicular distance to the pivot (or center of gravity); a torque produces rotation the way a force produces translation. Week 8.
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: Speed of Sound
sources.description: On a standard sea-level day sound travels about 1,100 feet per second (761 mph); speed depends on temperature. Week 3 (ultrasonic distance sensor).
sources.license: NASA media guidelines: generally not subject to US copyright; credit NASA. https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

sources.title: 4.4 Newton's Third Law of Motion, Physics (high school)
sources.publisher: OpenStax (Rice University) and Texas Education Agency
sources.description: Every force has an equal and opposite partner force on the other object. Week 7.
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer, checked 2026-10-27; adapt with credit per D307 in a marked block)

sources.title: 10.6 Torque, University Physics Volume 1
sources.description: Torque grows with the force and with the lever arm. Week 8 (teacher background; the lesson stays qualitative).
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer, checked 2026-10-27; adapt with credit per D307 in a marked block)

sources.title: MS-PS2-1 Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions
sources.description: Performance expectation: apply Newton's third law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects. Weeks 7 and 11.

sources.title: MS-ETS1-4 Engineering Design
sources.description: Performance expectation: develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a design. Weeks 5 and 11.

sources.title: Recreational Flyers & Community-Based Organizations
sources.description: Recreational rules under 49 USC 44809: fly only for fun; follow a recognized CBO's safety guidelines; keep the drone in visual line of sight; at or below 400 feet in Class G airspace; authorization in controlled airspace; pass TRUST; register and mark if required; Remote ID. Week 10.

sources.title: The Recreational UAS Safety Test (TRUST)
sources.description: Recreational flyers must pass TRUST before flying; the online test is free through FAA-approved administrators; answers are correctable to 100 percent; keep the certificate. Week 10.

sources.title: How to Register Your Drone
sources.description: All drones must be registered except those 0.55 lb (250 g) or less flown under the recreational exception; the registrant must be 13 or older, so a younger owner needs someone 13 or older to register. Week 10.

sources.title: Remote Identification of Drones
sources.description: Remote ID broadcasts a drone's identification and location; required for drones that must be registered; FRIAs. Week 10.

sources.title: B4UFLY
sources.description: The FAA's B4UFLY service shows recreational flyers where they can and cannot fly. Week 10.

sources.title: Educational Users
sources.description: How drones flown for school are regulated (44809 or Part 107); schools below college level must be chartered by a recognized CBO to fly under 44809; schools can request a FRIA. Week 10 grown-up note.

sources.title: No Drone Zone
sources.description: No Drone Zones, restricted airspace, local takeoff and landing limits, and Temporary Flight Restrictions (for example major sporting events). Week 10.

sources.title: Safety (AMA safety handbook)
sources.description: The AMA safety handbook; the AMA is an FAA-recognized community-based organization and administers TRUST. Week 10 grown-up note.
